title: Finding Noise
coreMove: Spot judgment variability as a systemic problem distinct from bias before asking which individual was wrong.
sourcePressure: An insurance company tested 48 underwriters on the same cases and found roughly 55 percent variability where it expected around 10 percent. The opening shock works because it makes disagreement visible and costly before any explanation about who is wrong. The chapter distinguishes bias (average error) from noise (variability in error) as fundamentally different problems.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating noise as just a synonym for bias, or assuming that finding the outlier in any disagreement fully resolves the problem.

sourceAnchors.name: The 48-underwriter insurance audit
sourceAnchors.detail: An insurance company tested 48 of its own underwriters on identical cases and found roughly 55 percent variability in their pricing — far above the roughly 10 percent the company expected. This is the book's opening anchor case.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Forty-eight underwriters pricing the same risk should not spread their answers by 55 percent. One insurance company discovered they did — and that the company itself had no idea.

hook: noise is a hidden problem that affects us all
you think you know how to judge — but do you?
counterintuition: experts disagree more than you think
bias is not the only problem in judgment
tryThisNow: set a timer and write down your first impression
think of a recent decision you made
examples: generic 'two experts disagree' scene with no institutional anchor
a scene that opens with the narrator explaining what noise is

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: The opening shock of ch01 needs variety to prevent readers from feeling they are watching the same institutional reveal six times in a row.

exampleSpecs.domain: insurance company running an internal quality audit of underwriter pricing
exampleSpecs.audience: a senior risk officer who commissioned the study believing the spread would be around 10 percent
exampleSpecs.stakes: the discovery that the company's pricing is far less consistent than management assumed, and that customers in identical situations are paying very different premiums
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the risk officer spreads the 48 quotes for the same policy on a conference table and the range from lowest to highest becomes visible as a physical object before any explanation is offered
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a row of printed quote sheets laid end to end across a long table, the numbers at the top of each page showing different figures
mustInclude: the gap between expected and actual variability
the moment the officer stops explaining and just looks
mustAvoid: implying any underwriter was negligent or dishonest

exampleSpecs.domain: psychiatric asylum determination board reviewing the same case file
exampleSpecs.audience: two psychiatrists who each believe they applied the standard criteria
exampleSpecs.stakes: a person's liberty and safety — an incorrect denial means return to danger, an incorrect approval creates a different risk
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: one psychiatrist reads her written assessment aloud and the other psychiatrist realizes he coded the identical file in the opposite direction, and neither has a clear explanation for why
exampleSpecs.firstImage: the same manila folder open on the table between two people with different handwritten notes on their own copies
mustInclude: no bad faith or negligence from either
mustAvoid: named countries or specific asylum procedures

exampleSpecs.domain: food safety inspection of a restaurant kitchen on the same day by two different inspectors
exampleSpecs.audience: a food safety manager trying to understand a complaint from the restaurant owner about inconsistent scoring
exampleSpecs.stakes: the restaurant's operating license and public health accountability, plus the credibility of the inspection system
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the manager places the two inspection reports side by side: the same kitchen, the same morning, one score a 94 and one a 67, and the discrepancy is not a typo
exampleSpecs.firstImage: two printed inspection forms with different scores in the top-right corner, placed face up on a desk
mustInclude: score gap that cannot be explained by different conditions
the moment the manager sees both numbers at once
mustAvoid: implying either inspector was bribed or careless
explaining the gap before showing it

exampleSpecs.domain: mortgage loan application assessed by two different loan officers at the same bank
exampleSpecs.audience: a bank quality officer reviewing a sample of borderline loan files
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a family gets a mortgage and at what rate — with downstream consequences for fair lending compliance
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: you are reviewing a loan file that two officers have already assessed: one approved it at a standard rate, one denied it, and you are the tiebreaker who realizes your own instinct points in a third direction
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a loan file with two sticky-note assessments in different handwriting, one saying approved and one saying declined
mustInclude: the three-way divergence that makes the systemic problem visible
mustAvoid: attributing the divergence to one officer's personal bias
resolving the tiebreaker — the point is the spread, not the answer

exampleSpecs.domain: pediatric radiology department reviewing diagnostic consistency in bone-age assessments
exampleSpecs.audience: a department chief conducting a routine accuracy review of X-ray reads across five pediatric radiologists
exampleSpecs.stakes: treatment timing decisions for growth disorders that depend on accurate bone-age estimates
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the department chief discovers that for a set of blind reads of the same X-rays, the spread across radiologists is nearly three years — far wider than the clinical decision threshold — and the reading she herself submitted is not at the center of the distribution
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a printed spreadsheet showing five columns of bone-age estimates, with the same X-ray ID in the first column and five different numbers across the row
mustInclude: blind read design (radiologists did not know they were being compared)
the chief's own estimate as part of the spread
the clinical significance of the spread relative to treatment decisions
mustAvoid: implying the radiologists were poorly trained

exampleSpecs.domain: school discipline incident reports reviewed by multiple vice-principals to calibrate suspension decisions
exampleSpecs.audience: a principal trying to understand why suspension rates vary across her three vice-principals for identical types of incident
exampleSpecs.stakes: students' educational continuity and the school's legal compliance with equal-treatment standards
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the principal hands the same anonymized incident report to all three vice-principals separately and asks for a recommended consequence; when she collects the answers, one recommends a verbal warning, one a three-day suspension, and one a five-day suspension — for the same incident
exampleSpecs.firstImage: three sealed envelopes the principal has not yet opened, each containing one vice-principal's written recommendation for the same report
mustInclude: same incident report, three different consequences
the principal's surprise at the range
the absence of obvious explanations in the individual answers
mustAvoid: picking one vice-principal as the correct one
explaining the spread before showing it

skillTargets: distinguish noise from bias given a scenario description
recognize when a pattern of disagreement reveals noise rather than one expert being wrong
apply the noise concept to an unfamiliar institution (outside insurance or courts)
analyze why average judgment can look acceptable while individual cases suffer from scatter
evaluate whether a proposed fix addresses noise or only addresses bias

tryThisNowSpec: Think of one recurring decision in your work — a hire, a rating, an approval — and write down the number you would give today. Now ask: if you had seen this case last Monday, or if a colleague saw it right now, would the number match? The gap you just imagined is a lower bound on the noise in that decision.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm — a direct second-person passage asking the reader to picture their own judgment system, or a brief research aside on the size of the underwriter spread relative to industry expectations
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
